summary:
Gibraltar stands under the United Kingdom framework with its own Parliament and Supreme Court which enact and interpret its civil and criminal law. United Kingdom legislation does not apply automatically in Gibraltar. The Secretary of State stated on 1 April 2010 that international obligations could be imposed by Order in Council.

No process exists in Gibraltar for changing a legal gender marker. The sourced material records that transgender persons are not permitted to change legal gender. A trans visitor therefore travels on a document whose marker cannot be altered by any local route.

The Equal Opportunities Act 2006 came into force on 1 March 2007 and prohibits discrimination in employment and in the provision of goods and services on grounds including gender reassignment. The Act defines gender reassignment as a process for the purpose of reassigning a person’s sex by changing physiological or other attributes of sex. The same Act prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation, defined as orientation towards persons of the same sex, the opposite sex, or both.

Male same-sex sexual activity was decriminalised in Gibraltar in 1993 following pressure from the European Court of Human Rights and the Government of the United Kingdom. No criminal prohibition relevant to same-sex conduct is recorded as remaining in force.

The Crimes Act 2011 was amended to criminalise hatred and harassment on the ground of sexual orientation. Parliament approved the bill on 19 September 2013, royal assent was given on 25 September and the provision took effect on 10 October 2013. In July 2026 Parliament passed a bill amending hate crime and hate speech legislation to include protections for transgender identity.

In July 2026 Parliament passed a bill making it an offence to offer or practice conversion therapy.

Gibraltar provides recognition for same-sex partnerships. Parliament passed a civil partnership law in March 2014 granting same-sex couples most rights of marriage including adoption as mandated by the 2013 ruling. The Civil Marriage Amendment Act 2016 was passed unanimously on 26 October 2016, received royal assent on 1 November and took effect on 15 December 2016, with the first marriage the next day. Where a deputy registrar opts out of officiating a same-sex marriage, an alternative registrar must be assigned.
tangentialFactors:
In July 2021 the Ministry for Justice and Equality began examining a proposal to make denigration of a person on the basis of sexual orientation a specific criminal offence. The review followed anti-gay abuse on social media during Pride month, which Chief Minister Fabian Picardo described as disgusting lurking homophobia. The Government stated it would monitor whether a specific offence was required.

The House of Commons Foreign Affairs Committee enquiry into overseas territories concluded in 2008 that discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender status should be made illegal in all overseas territories. The Committee’s Seventh Report for 2007-08 set accountability and good-governance expectations applicable to Gibraltar.

The Constitution adopted in 2006 does not mention sexual orientation. Proposals raised in 2002 to include it were omitted.
localsOnly:
The Supreme Court of Gibraltar ruled on 10 April 2013 that section 5(2) of the Adoption Act 1951 violated the Gibraltar Constitution, in effect legalising LGBT adoption as a matter of law. The Government gave effect to the ruling through the 2014 civil partnership legislation. The Adoption Act 2023 took full effect on 18 April 2024 and explicitly allows same-sex couples to adopt children without discrimination.

In February 2021 Gibraltar enacted a surrogacy law permitting non-commercial, altruistic surrogacy for married couples or civil partners unable to conceive. Children of same-sex couples conceived through artificial insemination receive automatic recognition.

In June 2017 the Gibraltar Health Authority approved an amendment to its in vitro fertilisation policy allowing lesbian couples to access assisted reproductive technology.
outOfScopeNotes:
Not sourced in the inventory are any entry or visa rules specific to trans persons, any border-screening procedures that risk outing, any bathroom or single-sex facilities law, and any rules on access to or restriction of gender-affirming care for visitors in Gibraltar.

Not sourced are the incidence or outcomes of trans-specific violence in Gibraltar and the enforcement practice following the July 2026 amendments on transgender identity hate crime and on conversion therapy.
